title: Use Every Ticket Exactly Once, in the Smallest Order

concept.title: Hierholzer's algorithm: walk until stuck, then splice in the detours while backing up
body: You have a pile of one-way plane tickets and must use **every ticket exactly once** in one trip that starts at airport 1. A trip that uses every edge of a graph exactly once is an *Euler path*; its existence was settled by Euler (the degrees must fit), and here it is guaranteed to exist. Among all valid trips print the one that is **smallest** when compared airport number by airport number.

*Hierholzer's algorithm* builds the trip. Keep a stack with the current walk. Look at the top airport `v`: if `v` still has an unused ticket, take the one to the **smallest** destination, remove it, and push that destination. If `v` has no unused ticket, the walk cannot continue from `v`: pop `v` and **add it to the trip** (the trip is built backwards). When the stack is empty, reverse the trip.

Why is the result the smallest? When a smallest-first walk gets stuck, the stuck airport must be the **end** of the whole trip (only it can have a missing outgoing ticket), and the detours explored on the way back are spliced in front of it in the right places. The loop is iterative, and every ticket is used once, so the time is O(m log m) with the sorting.

statement: There are `m` one-way tickets between airports numbered 1 to `n`. A trip starts at airport 1 and uses every ticket exactly once (it is guaranteed that such a trip exists). Among all such trips print the one whose sequence of airports is smallest in the lexicographic order (compare the first airports, then the second, and so on). Print the `m + 1` airports of the trip.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of airports (numbered 1 to n) and the number of tickets.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: a ticket for a flight from `u` to `v`.
outputFormat: The airports of the trip on one line.
constraints: Several tickets can be equal, and a ticket can go from an airport to itself.
It is guaranteed that all tickets can be used exactly once in a trip that starts at airport 1.

examples.note: The trips 1 2 3 1 4 1 and 1 4 1 2 3 1 both use all tickets; the smaller one is 1 2 3 1 4 1.

hints: Sort the destinations of every airport and always take the smallest unused ticket.
Keep a stack of the current walk; when the top airport has no tickets left, move it to the finished trip.
The finished trip is built backwards: reverse it at the end.

explanation: Hierholzer's algorithm with the destinations sorted so that the smallest is taken first: airports with no tickets left are moved from the stack to the trip, which is reversed at the end.
solution.complexity: Time O(m log m), space O(n + m).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
tickets = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
for u, v in tickets:
    adj[u].append(v)
for lst in adj:
    lst.sort(reverse=True)
stack = [1]
trip = []
while stack:
    v = stack[-1]
    if adj[v]:
        stack.append(adj[v].pop())
    else:
        trip.append(stack.pop())
trip.reverse()
print(*trip)
